title: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The movements of a plasmodium (Aethalium) towards damp, warm or nutritious spots and away from sugar or salt solutions can each be accounted for by local changes of surface tension, as in inanimate drops moving on a warmed or chemically altered surface.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: When we find that a plasmodium of Aethalium, for instance, creeps towards a damp spot, or towards a warm spot, or towards substances that happen to be nutritious, and again creeps away from solutions of sugar or of salt, we seem to be dealing with phenomena every one of which can be paralleled by ordinary phenomena of surface tension

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba”. Scope: slime-mould plasmodia and amoeboid organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-05: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The mechanism can be tested by separating tension gradients from biochemical sensing. Existing public movies offer behavioral proxies but lack the calibrated, orthogonal perturbations needed to resolve the causal account.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure spatial surface-tension gradients and plasmodial flow during controlled moisture, temperature, nutrient, sugar, and salt gradients, then perturb tension independently of sensory signaling. Support requires direction and speed to follow tension gradients and persist when canonical sensing is blocked.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public data rarely pair all stimuli with interfacial-tension measurements.

Chemotaxis and osmotaxis provide plausible active rivals.

Aethalium-specific data are sparse.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.4
data adequacy: 0.25
discriminating power: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.4

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Each taxis Thompson names has been recorded, so the behavioural parallel with inanimate drops can be illustrated. The account that local surface tension is the cause is not distinguished by those paths from sensory signalling. A discriminating test needs tension fields during the taxis, which remain unpublished as a usable series.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For plasmodial movement toward damp, warm or nutritious sites and away from sugar or salt, measure local surface tension and test whether the tension gradient predicts direction as it does for an inanimate drop. Movement up the tension gradient predicted by each stimulus would support the claim; movement that persists when surface tension is uniform would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Behavioural trajectories are common; simultaneous surface-tension maps are not.

Chemotaxis and thermotaxis signalling predict the same directions.

Sugar and salt change osmosis, viscosity and membrane state together.
